title: The Polite Way To Avoid a Hard Conversation
author: Chiarelli, Andrea
summary: Andrea Chiarelli examines how the feedforward technique -- Marshall Goldsmith's future-focused coaching methodology designed to lower defensiveness in development conversations -- is routinely misused by managers to avoid accountability conversations they find difficult. The article identifies the mechanism with precision: feedforward works by removing reference to the past, which strips the thing people defend; but this same removal strips accountability when accountability is what's required. Four specific avoidance patterns are named and explained: the pre-emptive pivot (opening the conversation in generic developmental terms to rule the specific incident out of bounds), the suggestion that only makes sense if you know the incident (plausible deniability as the feature), temporal vagueness (framing suggestions for 'stakeholder conversations generally' to avoid naming the specific failure), and the group-setting deflection (raising an individual problem in a team workshop). Throughout, Chiarelli is clear about who pays for these patterns: the team member is deprived of clear, specific information about what went wrong and what they should do differently. The article ends with practical guidance on when feedforward genuinely serves development (ongoing skill-building, routine coaching) versus when direct feedback about a specific incident is what's actually needed.
points: The same mechanism that makes feedforward useful in development conversations -- removing past behaviour as the subject -- makes it harmful when misapplied to accountability situations where what happened is precisely what needs to be named.

The pre-emptive pivot is the most common avoidance pattern: opening the conversation in generic developmental terms effectively rules the specific incident out of bounds for the rest of the meeting, because raising it afterward would require abandoning the frame just set up.

Temporal vagueness -- framing feedback for 'stakeholder conversations going forward' rather than 'the meeting last Tuesday' -- lets managers gesture at a specific failure while maintaining deniability that they were addressing it, leaving the receiver to guess.

The true cost of avoidance falls on the team member: they are deprived of the specific, clear information they need to understand what went wrong and make a different choice next time -- which is the stated purpose of any feedback conversation.

Feedforward genuinely belongs in conversations about ongoing skill development and character growth; it is not a technique for addressing specific incidents, and using it there is a category error that serves the giver's comfort more than the receiver's development.
quotes: Something specific has gone wrong with a team member's work, like a missed deadline, say, or a client meeting that didn't land. And you know you need to raise it. You sit down with them, and somehow the conversation ends up being about general development, or how similar situations might be handled in future, rather than about the thing itself.

The legitimate case for feedforward is strong. It lowers defensiveness, because there is nothing to defend yet. It is easier on both parties, because no one has to deliver a judgement about something the other person did.

The same mechanism that strips out friction in a development conversation also strips out accountability when accountability is what's required. When something specific has gone wrong, the future-oriented frame removes the very thing that needs to be acknowledged.

By starting in general terms, the manager has effectively ruled the specific event out of bounds for the rest of the conversation, because raising it now would mean abandoning the frame they have just set up.

It is worth being clear about who pays for avoidance: taking away feedback conversations deprives the team member of clear and specific information that they need to make sense of what happened and to do something different next time.
In all these cases, the receiver can usually work out what the conversation is really about, often within the first few minutes. Which means the giver has achieved neither clarity nor kindness.
